summary:
FMLink reports that BOMA International, the commercial real estate trade association, is promoting its Legionella / Legionnaires' disease guidance following a Legionnaires' outbreak in New York City. City health officials say the outbreak source has been identified and remediated after extensive testing and disinfection. The outbreak produced dozens of reported cases and several deaths, which BOMA frames as evidence of the need for proactive building water system management.

BOMA Chair and Chief Elected Officer Kjersten Jaeb (BOMA Fellow, RPA, LEED GA) says that although health officials have contained the immediate threat, Legionella prevention requires ongoing vigilance, and that building owners and managers play a critical role in maintaining safe water systems. BOMA positions itself as committed to supplying supporting resources.

The article explains the underlying condition: Legionnaires' disease is a serious form of pneumonia caused by Legionella bacteria. It is not transmitted person to person and cannot be contracted by drinking water. Infection happens when people inhale aerosolized water droplets containing the bacteria. Those droplets can form in building systems such as cooling towers, hot water systems, decorative fountains, and other water features.

BOMA stresses that despite the outbreak being localized to New York City, Legionella risk management is a nationwide concern for building owners and operators. The association offers comprehensive guidance and best practices for preventing, identifying, and responding to Legionella-related risks, published as a downloadable Legionella Guidance Document linked from the piece.

The item is essentially an industry association resource announcement aimed at facilities, property management, and commercial real estate audiences, tying a public health incident to routine water management compliance and preventive maintenance responsibilities. It contains no product, technology, workplace-policy, or workplace-experience content beyond building operations and environmental health and safety.
